title: The Author’s Way of Sending Forth His Second Part of the Pilgrim

v: Go now, my little book, to every place
where my first Pilgrim ever showed his face.
Call at their door. If any say, “Who’s there?”
then answer them, “Christiana is here.”
If they invite you in, then enter, bring
your boys along, and tell them everything:
who these are, and the place they started from;
perhaps they’ll know them by their looks, or name.
But if they don’t, then ask them once again
whether they did not, some time back, take in
one Christian, a pilgrim. If they say
they did, and were delighted with his way,
then let them know that these are his, his own:
his wife and children, following where he’s gone.
Tell them that they have left their house and home,
have turned to pilgrims, seeking a world to come;
that they have met with hardships on the way,
that troubles meet them still by night and day;
that they have trod on serpents, fought with devils,
and overcome a great many evils.
Yes, tell them also of the rest, who have,
for love of pilgrimage, been stout and brave
defenders of that road, and how they still
refuse this world, to do their Father’s will.
Go, tell them too of all the lovely things
that pilgrimage to every pilgrim brings.
And let them learn as well how much they are
beloved of their King, and in his care:
what goodly mansions he for them provides,
though they meet with rough winds and swelling tides;
how fine a calm they will enjoy at last
who to their Lord, and to his ways, hold fast.
Perhaps with heart and hand they will embrace
you, as they did my firstborn, and will grace
you and your fellows with such cheer and fare
as shows that lovers of pilgrims they are.
But what if they will not believe that I
am truly yours? For there are some who try
to counterfeit the Pilgrim and his name,
and by disguise to seem the very same,
and by that trick have wormed their way into
the hands and houses of I don’t know who.
It’s true that some have lately tried to cheat:
to counterfeit my Pilgrim, and to set
my title on their own; and others, too,
have stitched half my name and title to
their books, to make them sell. But by their face
they show they are not mine, nor of my race.
If you meet such, then this is your one way:
before them all, stand up and say your say
in your own native language, which no man
now uses, or can counterfeit; and then,
if after all they still should doubt you, and
think that, like gypsies, you roam through the land
in wicked ways, the country to defile,
or that you seek good people to beguile
with things not warranted, then send for me,
and I will testify that you must be
my pilgrims; yes, I’ll testify that you,
and only you, are mine. That much will do.
But what if I inquire for him from those
who wish him damned, body and soul, his foes?
What shall I do when I, at such a door,
ask after pilgrims, and they rage the more?
My book, don’t frighten yourself; bugbears like these
are only grounds for groundless fears. With ease
my Pilgrim’s book has traveled sea and land,
and never yet could I come to understand
that it was slighted, or turned out of door,
by any kingdom, whether rich or poor.
In France and Flanders, where men kill each other,
my Pilgrim is esteemed a friend, a brother.
In Holland too, it’s said, as I am told,
my Pilgrim is to some worth more than gold.
Highlanders and the wild Irish both agree
my Pilgrim’s welcome in their company.
In New England he’s been so far advanced,
received with so much love, that he’s enhanced:
they’ve trimmed him, newly clothed him, decked with gems,
so he may show his features and his limbs.
And more: so handsomely my Pilgrim walks
that thousands daily sing of him, and talk.
If you draw nearer home, it will appear
my Pilgrim knows no ground for shame or fear;
city and country both will entertain
him with a “Welcome, Pilgrim!”; they can’t refrain
from smiling if my Pilgrim’s standing by,
or shows his head in any company.
Brave gallants hug my Pilgrim, and they love
and prize him greatly; value him above
things of a greater bulk; yes, with delight
they say, “A lark’s leg’s better than a kite.”
Young ladies and young gentlewomen show
my Pilgrim no small kindness, as I know.
Their cabinets, their bosoms, and their hearts
my Pilgrim has, because to them he imparts
his pretty riddles in such wholesome strains
as yield them profit double to their pains
of reading; yes, I think I may be bold
to say some prize him far above their gold.
The very children playing in the street,
if they should chance my holy Pilgrim to meet,
salute him well, wish him well, and will say
he is the only stripling of the day.
Those who have never seen him still admire
what they have heard of him, and much desire
to have his company, and hear him tell
those pilgrim stories which he knows so well.
Yes, some who did not love him at the first,
but called him fool and dunce, say that they must,
now that they’ve seen and heard him, recommend
him, and to those they love they gladly send.
Therefore, my Second Part, you need not fear
to show your head; none can do you harm here
who wished the first one well, since you come after
bearing a second store of just that matter:
things just as good, as rich, as profitable,
for young, for old, for staggering, and for stable.
But some there are who say he laughs too loud,
and some who say his head is in a cloud;
some say his words and stories are so dark
they don’t know how, by them, to find his mark.
One may, I think, say both his laughs and cries
may well be guessed at by his watery eyes.
Some things are of a nature that will make
one’s fancy chuckle while one’s heart does ache.
When Jacob saw his Rachel with the sheep,
he did at the same moment kiss and weep.
As for those who say a cloud is in his head,
that only shows how wisdom goes, instead,
wrapped in her own mantles, to stir the mind
to search for what it so much longs to find.
Things that seem hidden in words dark, obscure,
only the more the godly mind allure
to study what those sayings must contain
that speak to us in such a cloudy strain.
I know, as well, a dark similitude
will on the imagination more intrude,
and stick far faster in the heart and head
than anything in plainer language said.
Therefore, my book, let no discouragement
hinder your travels. See, you have been sent
to friends, not foes; to friends who will give place
to you, your pilgrims, and your words embrace.
Besides, what my first Pilgrim left concealed,
you, my brave second Pilgrim, have revealed;
what Christian left locked up and went his way,
sweet Christiana opens with her key.
But some don’t like the method of your first;
they call it a romance, and toss it as dust.
If I should run across such people, what
should I do: slight them as they slight me, or not?
My Christiana, if you meet with these,
by all means greet them lovingly; and please,
don’t give them back reviling for revile;
but if they frown, I beg you, simply smile.
Perhaps it’s nature, or some ill report,
that’s made them so despise, or so retort.
Some love no cheese, some love no fish, and some
don’t love their friends, or their own house and home;
some start at pork, slight chicken, don’t love fowl
more than they love a cuckoo or an owl.
Leave such, my Christiana, to their choice,
and seek out those who’ll find you and rejoice;
by no means strive, but humbly, as is wise,
present yourself to them in pilgrim’s guise.
Go then, my little book, and show to all
who welcome you and take you in, the whole
of what you keep shut up from all the rest;
and wish that what you show them may be blest
to them for good, and make them choose to be
pilgrims far better than you or me.
Go then, I say; tell all men, from the heart,
“I am Christiana, and my part
is now, with my four sons, to tell you what
it is for men to take a pilgrim’s lot.”
Go, tell them also who they are, these who
now go on pilgrimage along with you;
say, “Here’s my neighbor Mercy; she has been
my fellow pilgrim since this road began.
Come, see her run her maiden race, and learn
the idle from the pilgrim to discern.”
Yes, let young women learn from her to see
the world to come as what their prize should be.
When little tripping maidens follow God,
and leave old doting sinners to his rod,
it’s like those days in which the young ones cried
“Hosanna!” to the One the old decried.
Next, tell them of old Honest, whom you found
with his white hairs, treading the pilgrim’s ground.
Yes, tell them how plain-hearted this man was,
how after his good Lord he bore his cross.
Perhaps with some gray head this may prevail
to fall in love with Christ, and his sins bewail.
Tell them also how Master Fearing went
on pilgrimage, and how his time was spent
in solitude, with many fears and cries;
and how at last he won the joyful prize.
He was a good man, though much down in spirit;
he is a good man, and does life inherit.
Tell them of Master Feeble-mind also,
who would not lead, but at the rear would go.
Show them how he was very nearly slain,
and how one Great-heart gave him life again.
This man was true of heart, though weak in grace;
one might read true godliness in his face.
Then tell of Master Ready-to-stumble, who
went on his crutches, yet was faultless too;
tell them how Master Feeble-mind and he
were loving friends, and would in most things agree.
And let all know, whatever their circumstance
of weakness, one could sing, the other dance.
Forget not Master Valiant-for-truth,
that man of courage, though a very youth.
Tell everyone his spirit was so stout
no man could ever make him turn about;
and how Great-heart and he could not forbear,
but pulled down Doubting Castle, and slew Despair.
Don’t overlook Master Despondency,
nor Much-afraid, his daughter, though they lie
under such coverings as make them seem
(to some) as if their God had forsaken them.
They softly went, but sure, and in the end
found that the Lord of pilgrims was their friend.
When you have told the world of all these things,
then turn about, my book, and touch these strings,
which, if but touched, will such sweet music make
they’ll make the lame man dance, a giant quake.
These riddles that lie couched within your breast,
freely propound, expound; and for the rest
of your mysterious lines, let them remain
for those whose nimble fancies can explain.
Now may this little book a blessing be
to those who love this little book and me;
and may its buyer have no cause to say
his money is but lost or thrown away;
yes, may this Second Pilgrim yield such fruit
as may each good pilgrim’s fancy suit;
and may it persuade some who go astray
to turn their feet and heart to the right way.
This is the hearty prayer of the Author,
